title: Redwood Structured Output & Function Calling Demo
summary: Redwood AE+SE demoed structured output (JSON mode), schema enforcement, and function/tool-calling flows via the API and Console. Customer (Acme Fintech) is evaluating for a POC to replace an internal LLM gateway with stronger guardrails around JSON outputs and deterministic tool calls for transaction enrichment. Questions on security (KMS, audit logs), latency tradeoffs with strict schema enforcement, and Dedicated/VPC deployment. Next steps: share POC scope, pricing, security pack, and schedule a 2-week pilot benchmark with sample prompts and data retention settings.
topics: Guardrails for invalid JSON and fallbacks
next_steps: Redwood to send POC scope & pricing (Maya)
Share security docs (SOC2, encryption, audit logs) (Liam)
Customer to provide sample prompt set and sample records for benchmark (Ethan)
Schedule 60-min benchmark kickoff for week of Sep 22 (calendar invite)
Follow-up demo on Dedicated/VPC options if POC requires private deployment (Maya)
action_items: Maya Chen: Send detailed POC scope and pricing by 2025-09-12
Liam Patel: Share security & architecture docs (SOC2, KMS, audit logs) and sample console video by 2025-09-12
Ethan Cole: Provide 100 sample prompts and 500 records for latency/accuracy benchmark by 2025-09-18
Priya Nair: Confirm internal stakeholders and success criteria by 2025-09-15
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, I'll kick us off, I have Liam from the SE team as well.
[00:06] Sofia Ramirez: Hi thanks, we got about 45 minutes. We're keen to see structured output and how function calling can make our downstream pipeline more deterministic.
[00:12] Liam Patel: Awesome, we built a demo focusing exactly on that — JSON mode with schemas, plus function calling so you can do enrichment without parsing heuristics. I'll share my screen.
[00:25] Tom Briggs: Quick note — we run in a regulated environment so VPC/private deploy and KMS are big for us.
[00:30] Maya Chen: Noted, we'll show both hosted API flows and what Dedicated/VPC looks like in the console.
[00:37] [02:05] Liam Patel: (screen) Alright starting with API — here's a normal generate call. If you set mode: "structured_json" and provide a schema, the runtime validates model output against that schema. If the model deviates we can retry, coerce, or emit an error you can capture.
[02:18] Ethan Cole: When it retries, is that another token cost? How does pricing work?
[02:23] Maya Chen: Good q — retries are additional tokens, but you can set a low-retry policy; also Redwood Optimize suggests batching/quantization and gives unit-cost estimates. We'll include a cost projection in the POC.
[02:35] Sofia Ramirez: Can you show a real example?
[02:39] Liam Patel: Sure. Example: provide a schema for a transaction enrichment response — fields: merchant, category, confidence (float), timestamp. I'll call the endpoint. 
[03:05] Liam Patel: (typing) We make the call, model returns, but intentionally returns confidence as "0,85" (comma) and extra field "note". In JSON mode the runtime notices schema mismatch — here we have three configured policies: 
[03:20] Liam Patel: 1) strict: reject and return error, 2) best-effort-coerce: attempt to coerce types (comma to dot), 3) fallback: call a secondary smaller model for correction.
[03:35] Priya Nair: That fallback is internal to Redwood runtime? Is it configurable?
[03:38] Liam Patel: Yes, it's part of routing policies. You can pin models or set automatic fallback to a quantized variant.
[03:44] [05:10] Maya Chen: I'll switch to function calling. The API supports explicit tool schemas so the model returns a call with name and arguments we map to an internal service.
[05:20] Maya Chen: For ex, model returns {"tool": "enrich_txn", "args": {"txn_id": "123"}} and Redwood will POST to your endpoint with auth headers.
[05:35] Ethan Cole: How do we guarantee idempotency and auth for those callbacks? We have strict access rules.
[05:40] Liam Patel: Callback requests include signed headers and can be routed through your VPC endpoint. For Dedicated/VPC we support mutual TLS and customer-managed KMS for signing. We'll add details in the security pack.
[05:52] [07:05] Sofia Ramirez: Is the tool-call synchronous? We sometimes need synchronous enrich because downstream pipeline expects immediate fields.
[07:12] Liam Patel: You can configure sync or async. If sync, Redwood waits for the tool response (within a configurable timeout), if async, we return a tracking id and webhook when complete.
[07:22] Tom Briggs: Timeout behavior — do you buffer KV cache while waiting? We can't lose state.
[07:28] Liam Patel: We maintain ephemeral KV caches per request; state is either returned or persisted to your store via the tool. We'll share architecture diagrams.
[07:35] [09:00] Maya Chen: Back to schema enforcement — we demoed coercion; now demo guardrails: you can reject outputs with PII, or require that enums match a canonical list.
[09:12] Liam Patel: Here's an example where model tries to fill in a "client_ssn" field — we have a policy that strips values and emits an redacted marker and writes an audit log.
[09:24] Priya Nair: Audit logs — are those delivered to our SIEM or available in the console only?
[09:29] Liam Patel: Logs can stream to your SIEM via syslog or Kafka connector; we also store them in the Redwood Console with retention controls. You control retention policies in Private/Dedicated.
[09:38] [11:00] Ethan Cole: A quick perf question: enforcing strict schemas and retries — what latency impact should we expect for 50–200ms SLO?
[11:07] Maya Chen: It depends; strict rejection path is fastest (fail fast), coercion adds a small parse step, fallback to another model adds model latency. For our benchmarks we'll show p50/p95 with and without strict schemas. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantized fallback models to meet latencies.
[11:27] Sofia Ramirez: Do you have benchmarks for our typical sequence lengths? Our calls are usually 256 tokens average.
[11:33] Liam Patel: We'll run a POC with your sample prompts. In console you can configure a perf profile per model and see token breakdown, cache hit rate, etc.
[11:42] [13:00] Maya Chen: Now switching to Console — higher-level view: routes, model pinning, rollouts, and structured output settings. Liam demoed how to attach a schema to a route.
[13:20] Liam Patel: (screen) In this route settings you can set enforce_schema: strict|coerce|none, and function_calling enabled, plus set the callback URL and headers. You can also preview sample responses in the console with schema validation diagnostics.
[13:40] Tom Briggs: Can we run the preview against our staging endpoint?
[13:44] Liam Patel: Yes, just add the staging webhook and use the VPC peering config; for hosted customers we provide secure tunnels for short-lived testing.
[13:50] [15:10] Sofia Ramirez: Another question — what happens if the schema evolves (new enum values)? How do we rollout schema changes safely?
[15:18] Maya Chen: You can version schemas and use canary traffic rules. Console has a schema diff view and you can route small percentage of traffic to the new schema, and Redwood will emit compatibility warnings in the traces.
[15:35] Priya Nair: Nice. On the security front, can you map audit events to our internal users (SSO)? We need RBAC mapping.
[15:42] Liam Patel: We integrate with SAML/SSO and have role mappings for Console actions; audit logs include user ids and action types. For Private deployments you can also push logs to your audit storage.
[15:54] [17:00] Ethan Cole: Are there any gotchas with JSON mode and chained tool calls? We sometimes do multi-step enrichment where model calls tool A, gets response, then calls tool B.
[17:10] Liam Patel: That works; we support nested function calls. The runtime can manage a call graph and apply schemas at each step. You can also define a guardrail: max call depth, total token budget, and prohibited tool list.
[17:24] Maya Chen: We often see customers worry about hallucinated tool calls — to prevent that you can restrict allowed tool names and require signed tool manifests.
[17:34] [19:00] Sofia Ramirez: Can Redwood block outputs containing banks or PII? We need to ensure no raw PHI/PII is returned to clients.
[19:07] Liam Patel: Yes, content filters and data scrubbing policies sit before response transmission; you can also configure transforms to redact fields and write original values to a secure audit blob if required.
[19:22] Priya Nair: For compliance we need encryption-at-rest + bring-your-own-key.
[19:26] Maya Chen: Supported — BYOK via KMS/HSM is supported for Private & Dedicated, hosted customers can use Redwood-managed KMS with customer KMS integration for certain tiers. We'll include details in the security docs.
[19:36] [21:00] Ethan Cole: Ok about operational tooling — we want to see cost breakdown per route.
[21:08] Liam Patel: Console exposes token cost per route, per model, and Optimize gives suggestions like switch to int8 quantized for certain traffic to save 40% cost while keeping >threshold accuracy.
[21:24] Sofia Ramirez: Any pre-built integrations for our data pipeline — Kafka, Snowflake?
[21:29] Maya Chen: We have connectors for Kafka and S3; Snowflake via batch export. For real-time enrichment we recommend tool-calls to your service.
[21:40] [23:00] Tom Briggs: About deployment modes — if we go Dedicated with reserved GPU pools, what commit levels do you usually see?
[23:08] Maya Chen: Typical mid-market commitment is 3–12 months with reserved throughput tiers. We can model expected throughput from your sample set.
[23:18] Ethan Cole: Another subtle point—kv cache size and eviction policy. Our sequences sometimes reuse prefixes.
[23:25] Liam Patel: Our serving runtime has configurable KV cache TTLs and shard-aware eviction; also caching is per-route and visible in console traces.
[23:34] [25:00] Maya Chen: Quick live test of a failing schema path — I'll run a prompt that purposely returns malformed JSON.
[25:10] Liam Patel: (typing) call in... model returns a trailing comma and stringified numbers. Console shows validation error, and we trigger a configured fallback to the small corrective model. It corrects in 120ms and returns coerced values, audit logged.
[25:30] Priya Nair: The correction model — is that a separate billing line?
[25:33] Maya Chen: Billed as part of the route execution; Optimize reports the extra cost and suggests tradeoffs. You can also set a hard cap to avoid unexpected cost.
[25:43] [27:00] Sofia Ramirez: If we need guaranteed determinism for some fields, can you pin a deterministic model? We have regulatory fields that must be canonicalized.
[27:10] Liam Patel: You can pin a specific model version; for stronger determinism we recommend ensemble patterns and schema strictness, plus logging to verify deterministic outputs.
[27:22] Tom Briggs: Any limitations on schema complexity — nested arrays, large object graphs?
[27:28] Liam Patel: We support nested JSON schemas; complexity can affect validation time but typically negligible unless extremely deep. We'll test with your real schemas.
[27:38] [29:00] Maya Chen: Quick run through of POC plan: 1) customer provides sample prompts, 2) Redwood sets up a scoped route in hosted or Dedicated staging, 3) run 1k requests across scenarios (strict, coerce, fallback), 4) produce perf/cost/accuracy report.
[29:18] Ethan Cole: Sounds good. We want to run the tests in our staging network if possible.
[29:22] Liam Patel: We'll request a staging webhook or VPC peering. If private deployment needed — we'll walk through Dedicated sizing.
[29:32] [31:00] Priya Nair: Regarding SSO and per-user RBAC, can we map actions to our internal teams and restrict who can change schemas?
[31:08] Maya Chen: Yes, RBAC rules allow schema-edit permissions separate from run permissions. We'll send a sample policy.
[31:18] Sofia Ramirez: What's the expected timeline to get a POC up and running?
[31:22] Maya Chen: Typically 1–2 weeks to stand up a scoped route and run benchmarks, depending on network access. We'll aim for kickoff week of Sep 22.
[31:34] [33:00] Ethan Cole: One last question on failure modes — if function-calling returns 500 from our service, does Redwood retry?
[33:08] Liam Patel: Retry policy is configurable per route: exponential backoff, max attempts, or immediate fail. All retries are audit logged and you can choose to queue via dead-letter.
[33:20] Tom Briggs: Great.
[33:25] [35:00] Maya Chen: Recap — we'll send POC scope + pricing, Liam will send security docs and console walkthrough recording, Ethan will supply sample prompts/records, Priya will confirm stakeholders.
[35:15] Sofia Ramirez: We'll also want a checklist for compliance items.
[35:19] Liam Patel: I'll include a compliance checklist (SOC2, encryption, audit log delivery, SSO config).
[35:26] [37:00] Maya Chen: Any blockers right now?
[37:05] Ethan Cole: Only internal approvals and we need to confirm if PII test data is allowed. We'll provide anonymized samples first.
[37:12] Priya Nair: We'll confirm date for kickoff.
[37:15] Maya Chen: Great.
[37:20] [39:00] Maya Chen: I'll follow up with an email with links: POC deck, pricing spreadsheet, security pack, and a calendar invite.
[39:10] Liam Patel: Links in chat: demo deck: https://redwood.ai/demo/deck, security pack: https://redwood.ai/security-pack, sample console video: https://redwood.ai/console-video (these are demo links).
[39:28] Sofia Ramirez: Thanks everyone.
[39:31] Ethan Cole: Thanks, that was helpful.
[39:35] [41:00] Maya Chen: Thanks all; we'll be in touch.
[41:10] [END]
